description: FDM material comparison for design decisions. Each field carries a tag: MEASURED (physical test with numbers), VENDOR (maker data sheet or guide), PRACTITIONER (experienced designer advice), DERIVED (worked out from a sourced fact), UNVERIFIED (not confirmed at a primary source), SNIPPET (seen only in a search excerpt). Vendor data sheets are often measured on annealed specimens or in a hot chamber; z.strength.fraction here is the conservative open-printer value. Temperatures in C; strains as fractions (0.02 = 2 percent); clearance.adjust.side is added PER SIDE to the profile's fit clearances. Recommendations, not limits; the user's stated material and data override them.

pla.name: PLA (standard, e.g. PLA Basic, PolyLite, Prusament)

z.strength.fraction.note: Standing hook 55 percent of flat; tensile coupons 49 percent (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7aJ4dDyyf20). Untuned stock profiles: 0.40 (pull ring) and 0.48 (bend), single samples (MEASURED, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a6m_GnN5j4c). Across-layer impact only about 0.23 to 0.26 of in-layer (same source; strength.z.impact.fraction in fdm.json). Bambu's annealed sheet shows 89 percent: do not use it.

heat.deflection.note: HDT at 0.45 MPa 55 to 60 C across Bambu, Polymaker, Prusament.

service.limit.note: 45 to 50 C under load; Bambu advises against environments at about 50 C; CNC Kitchen oven test gave way at 60 C. Fails in a parked car.

creep.note: Worst of the common rigid materials in a short-term creep study (91 um vs PC 3 um at 10 MPa, 3 h). Avoid sustained preload.

snapfit.strain.onetime.note: Derived from data-sheet strain with the molding 70 percent rule, then halved for layer lines.

enclosure.note: Open the door or lid on an enclosed printer when the bed is over 45 C.

ease.rank.note: 1 easiest; a judgment from Bambu requirements and CNC Kitchen experience, not a measurement.

clearance.adjust.side.note: Baseline: sliding 0.15 to 0.25 per side for PLA.

pla.notes: House default. Stiffest and strongest in XY of the common materials, lowest shrink (about 0.3 percent, secondary sources), brittle in impact and in notches. Hotter is not stronger: Z strength was best near the default (about 215 C) and dropped at 195 C and above about 255 C (MEASURED, Prusament on an MK3, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YJdkE7A8stM). Annealing raises heat resistance but distorts parts up to 10 percent and does not raise layer adhesion (CNC Kitchen).

pla-tough.name: PLA Tough+ / impact-modified PLA

z.strength.fraction.note: Vendor annealed value is 60 percent; no open-printer test found, so assume no better than PLA.

creep.note: Modified PLA crept in CNC Kitchen's bolt-preload test; impact modifiers trade stiffness and creep for toughness.

snapfit.strain.repeated.source: derived: 60 percent rule applied to the one-time value is about 1.2 percent; 1 percent kept

pla-tough.notes: About 3x the unnotched and 9x the notched impact of PLA Basic in the vendor sheet, but softer (modulus 1860 vs 2580 MPa). Good for clips and snap fits at room temperature; not for sustained preload. 'PLA+' is not a standard; other vendors' grades vary.

pla-matte.name: PLA Matte / Silk (appearance grades)

z.strength.fraction.note: Across-layer impact is half or less of PLA Basic (Z Charpy 6.6 matte, 4.6 silk vs 13.8 kJ/m2, VENDOR); treat Z strength as poor.

snapfit.strain.onetime.note: Avoid for snap fits, thin flexing arms and Z-loaded features.

pla-matte.notes: Appearance parts only. Matte hides layer lines; silk's sheen exaggerates them.

pla-cf.name: PLA-CF (carbon-fiber filled PLA)

z.strength.fraction.note: Vendor annealed value 68 percent; fiber adds little across layers and Z impact is lower than PLA (7.8 vs 13.8 kJ/m2).

hardened.nozzle.note: 0.2 mm nozzle not compatible; 0.4 hardened acceptable for Bambu PLA-CF, 0.6 preferred for generic CF.

pla-cf.notes: About 35 percent stiffer in bending than PLA Basic, matte finish, dimensionally stable at room temperature. Not for heat, not for impact.

petg.name: PETG

z.strength.fraction.note: Standing hook 46 percent of flat on an open printer. For an unknown or untuned printer use 0.35 (pull ring on a stock profile, single sample, MEASURED, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a6m_GnN5j4c). Across-layer impact about 0.23 to 0.31 of in-layer (same source). Vendor sheets show 69 to 84 percent.

heat.deflection.note: 68 to 78 C by brand; CNC Kitchen sag test gave way at 80 C.

creep.note: Tested as CPE, a copolyester close to PETG: 33 um vs PLA 91 um at 10 MPa, 3 h.

enclosure.note: Not required; a cold room lowers layer strength.

ease.rank.note: Strings more than PLA, bonds hard to smooth PEI (use glue), same-material supports fuse.

clearance.adjust.side.note: Sliding 0.2 to 0.3 per side for PETG vs 0.15 to 0.25 for PLA. PETG oozes, so holes print slightly small.

petg.notes: About 70 percent of PLA's flexural stiffness: scale a bending section by about 1.12 for equal stiffness (a one-sample spring test found about 22 percent less stiff, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8_adY2K-YIc; the conservative 30 percent is kept). Heat-set inserts hold less in PETG than in PLA; self-tapping inserts or deeper engagement are stronger (MEASURED, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lYXTiJo_FQQ). Print at the filament's default temperature: PETG printed at 230 C bonded its layers worse than at 250 C, while hotter than default did not help PLA (MEASURED, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YJdkE7A8stM). Ductile under slow load (stretches rather than snaps), only modestly better in notched impact. Safer second default for functional parts of unknown use.

pctg.name: PCTG

heat.deflection.note: Secondary transcription of a producer sheet.

snapfit.strain.onetime.source: assumed at least PETG; elongation at break 24 percent per https://filamentcompare.com/pctg-vs-petg/

pctg.notes: A tougher, clearer PETG by vendor claim (impact 8 to 12x PETG claimed, UNVERIFIED). Choose over PETG for impact-loaded or clear parts; otherwise PETG rules.

petg-cf.name: PETG-CF

z.strength.fraction.note: Z impact equal to PETG (10.7 kJ/m2, VENDOR); no Z gain.

hardened.nozzle.note: 0.2 mm not compatible; AMS yes, AMS lite not recommended.

petg-cf.notes: Bending modulus about 50 percent above PETG Basic; matte finish; no meaningful heat or Z gain.

abs.name: ABS

z.strength.fraction.note: 54 percent open, 75 percent in a 65 C chamber: use 0.7 only on a printer with an actively heated chamber. Vendor 85 to 89 percent assumes annealed or 90 C chamber specimens.

service.limit.note: 80 to 85 C. Car cabins yes; dashboards in strong sun marginal.

creep.note: 64 um vs PLA 91 and PC 3 at 10 MPa, 3 h.

snapfit.strain.onetime.source: derived from https://www.fictiv.com/articles/how-to-design-snap-fit-components (SNIPPET: molded ABS about 7 percent, Z-built beams lose about half)
snapfit.strain.onetime.note: Conservative FDM value for XY beams; halve for beams bending across layers.

snapfit.strain.repeated.source: 60 percent of one-time (Bayer example, SNIPPET; Bayer/Covestro snap-fit guide, university-hosted copy listed as source 54 in docs/specs/dfm-research/04-hardware-fits-calibration.md (URL not repeated: its path carries a personal name))

enclosure.note: Not compatible with open Bambu printers.

clearance.adjust.side.note: Source gives +0.05 to +0.1 per side for ASA/ABS; the larger is used.

abs.notes: Shrink about 0.8 percent (secondary). Round footprint corners, add brims, keep walls under 6 loops and infill under 50 percent (Bambu warping advice). Acetone smoothable. Not UV stable: use ASA outdoors.

asa.name: ASA

z.strength.fraction.note: 29 percent on an open printer; a 30 C enclosure raised it by 20 percent. About 0.6 with a heated chamber is an UNVERIFIED interpolation. Bambu's sheet shows 84 percent.

service.limit.note: Oven test gave way at 110 C.

creep.note: Grouped with PLA and PA12 in CNC Kitchen's bolt-preload test.

enclosure.note: Prusament ASA printed acceptably open (CNC Kitchen), but Bambu requires an enclosure.

clearance.adjust.side.note: Sliding 0.25 to 0.35 per side for ASA vs 0.15 to 0.25 for PLA.

asa.notes: The outdoor material (about 85 percent tensile retained after 2000 h accelerated UV, equipment-vendor summary). Lowest across-layer impact of the common materials on open printers: reorient or thicken Z-loaded features.

tpu-95a.name: TPU 95A

service.limit.note: Softens gradually; not a rigid part near heat.

creep.source: general elastomer behavior; no data sheet value

snapfit.strain.onetime.note: Elastic (over 480 percent elongation across layers); snap-fit strain limits do not apply.

ease.rank.note: Slow, must be dry, not in the AMS (except TPU for AMS).

clearance.adjust.side.note: Flexible parts deform into fits; prove with a coupon.

tpu-95a.notes: Bridges only about 20 mm and overhang about 55 deg (VENDOR). Wall count and infill set softness. Use as the flexing half of a two-material part. Gaskets: 15 to 30 percent compression is general seal practice (UNVERIFIED).

pa6-cf.name: PA6-CF (carbon-fiber nylon 6)

z.strength.fraction.note: 47 percent dry and annealed; fiber reinforces only the layer plane.

service.limit.note: Oven test softened PA6 at 195 C.

creep.note: Unannealed bolt joint needed retightening almost daily; annealing at 110 C for 8 h greatly reduced creep.

snapfit.strain.onetime.note: CF-filled nylon is not for flexing.

drying.value: required, 80 C for 8 to 12 h, keep under 20 percent RH

clearance.adjust.side.note: Size holes after moisture conditioning, or ream.

pa6-cf.notes: Design to WET properties: in humid air stiffness fell to about one third and strength to about 56 percent of dry (MEASURED, CNC Kitchen). PA12-CF or PAHT-CF when stiffness must hold.

paht-cf.name: PAHT-CF (high-temperature carbon-fiber nylon)

creep.note: Wet bending strength 115 vs 76 MPa for generic PA6-CF.

paht-cf.notes: Holds stiffness better when wet than PA6-CF (wet bending modulus 3640 vs 2210 MPa, VENDOR).

pa-unfilled.name: Unfilled nylon (PA12, PA6)

creep.note: Largest elongation of the tested polymers.

snapfit.strain.onetime.source: https://www.fictiv.com/articles/how-to-design-snap-fit-components (SNIPPET, 4 to 15 percent printed nylon; BASF molded PA6 uses 4 percent for mating force)

ease.rank.note: Warps (shrink about 1.5 percent, secondary) and absorbs moisture.

pa-unfilled.notes: Best FDM choice with PP for living hinges and repeated snap fits (https://www.hubs.com/knowledge-base/how-design-living-hinges-3d-printing/); wear and sliding parts (PA12 is more moisture-stable than PA6).

pc.name: PC and PC blends

z.strength.fraction.note: PC Blend 65 percent open, 72 passive enclosure, 77 at 65 C chamber. Vendor 78 to 90 percent.

creep.note: 3 um at 10 MPa, 3 h. Best for clamped joints and inserts under sustained load.

snapfit.strain.onetime.source: conservative FDM value; BASF molded PC 4 to 9.2 percent (SNIPPET)

ease.rank.note: High temperatures, warps, needs a stress-relief anneal soon after printing (Polymaker).

pc.notes: Bambu PC FR is rated V-0 (thickness not captured, UNVERIFIED). Generous footprint radii, brim (4 mm over 5 cm for Prusament PC Blend), low fan.

pp.name: PP (polypropylene)

snapfit.strain.onetime.note: Best FDM material for living hinges, as thin as 0.4 mm.

ease.rank.note: Poor bed adhesion (needs a PP sheet or tape), shrink 1 to 3 percent (secondary), 25 to 35 mm brims.

pp.notes: Hinge 0.4 to 0.6 mm with the hinge line a continuous strand in the layer plane. Excellent chemical resistance.

pva.name: PVA (water-soluble support)

drying.value: required and kept sealed (absorbs 6.25 percent water)

pva.notes: Lets internal channels and flat undersides print clean on a multi-material printer; dissolve in water no hotter than 50 C when it supports PLA (https://us.store.bambulab.com/products/pva, SNIPPET). Costs print time, purge and drying.
